item.title: Imaging after a changed obstruction course
fairness: The new persistent localized pain requires interpretation despite maintained blood pressure, normal lactate and the initially reassuring scan. The second decision distinguishes a transit study from renewed assessment of anatomy and enhancement, making intravenous-contrast CT the best offered imaging plan.

The 48-hour interval makes a contrast transit assessment a credible wrong-stage choice. Noncontrast CT is a recognizable alternative but does not supply the same enhancement information. The task appropriately asks which imaging plan to use, rather than claiming that imaging must precede surgery in every deteriorating patient.

No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The explanation correctly avoids treating normal lactate as exclusion of threatened bowel and separates transit information from viability. The absence of guarding or rebound helps define the present decision without hiding emergency findings.

No reliable wording-only shortcut was found. The CT alternatives have parallel labels and the task does not name perfusion, intravenous contrast or a diagnostic conclusion. The shared words 'intravenous' and 'contrast' do not uniquely identify the answer.

The node follows the initial nonoperative decision coherently. Its update restates the admission imaging, treatment and changed course, so it is understandable with the shared presentation even when the preceding question is not shown. The preceding explanation does not rehearse this specific imaging answer.

Reassessing evolving obstruction and understanding the limits of reassuring laboratory findings are high-yield resident concepts. The difficulty is moderate because the reassuring findings and expected transit-testing stage compete with the new clinical change, not because information is withheld.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between the earlier scan and the new localized pain, the raw examination findings and the neutral imaging task. PASS is editorial only and does not constitute clinical approval.

item.title: Initial treatment of oliguria with fluid accumulation
fairness: The best offered treatment is IV furosemide for decongestion. Weight gain, new pulmonary findings and absent stroke-volume response must be integrated before choosing a diuretic rather than further fluid or immediate extracorporeal support. This is a common postoperative AKI management distinction.

Catheter patency, preserved circulation, modest current oxygen support and controlled potassium/pH supply the important competing-treatment context. The explanation appropriately identifies decongestion as the purpose; it does not claim that diuretics reverse kidney injury.

The ineffective crystalloid challenge is legitimate response evidence, not an answer-specific teaching sentence. The options are concrete and comparable treatment actions; no decisive wording, length, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut was found.
The named patient, age, sex and short complaint are present. The clinic frame clearly refers to a hospital decision, and the first node needs no previous answer.

Review scope: all nine current executable proposedNodes were independently assessed using their current presentation, update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation, including visible prior feedback. Author self-assessments and prior PASS labels were not evidence of quality. Two parked comparisons, three unkeyed slots, three withheld teaching points and one withdrawn candidate were noted but not scored; the assignment has no kept-unchanged or retired inventory rows. This is an offline editorial review, not fresh source verification or clinical approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative; every draft remains needs_clinician_review. Runtime randomization, timing metadata and actual rendering were outside the requested visible-text review.
suggestions: No substantive repair required. Optional feedback refinement: explicitly distinguish relieving congestion from improving renal recovery, and briefly explain why the current presentation permits a diuretic trial before kidney replacement.

Across the packet, the repeated clinic/referring-hospital framing can be shortened without obscuring where care occurs. Keep each separated task complete and retain the patient's demographics. This repetition alone does not invalidate a question.

item.title: Kidney-replacement decision after metabolic improvement
fairness: Serial chemistry and fluid-balance assessment is the best offered plan. The marked creatinine rise and oliguria create a real temptation to initiate replacement; the response of potassium/pH and the current organ-support findings instead support continued reassessment.

This requires separating injury severity from a current extracorporeal support indication, then choosing surveillance rather than immediate replacement or a prognostic stress test. It is high-yield moderate application, not evidence that a particular creatinine value is safe indefinitely.

The furosemide stress test addresses prognosis rather than replacing assessment of current complications. No additional immediate dialysis indication is supplied. The key and explanation retain reassessment rather than declaring the patient recovered.

The alternatives are different plans at the present decision point, with comparable label length and no uniquely explanatory key. Improved values are necessary clinical response data, not a nonmedical wording giveaway.
The first node stands alone. Its explanation teaches the distinction between injury and support need without naming the next node's pulmonary-fluid treatment answer.
suggestions: No required repair. A short post-answer sentence explaining the prognostic role of the furosemide stress test would make the closest test-selection error more instructive.

item.title: Escalation for pulmonary fluid accumulation despite diuretics
fairness: Urgent kidney replacement with fluid removal is the best offered escalation. The resident must connect accumulating balance and minimal urine to the pulmonary deterioration, then use the failed escalated loop-diuretic course and major hypoxemia to reject another pharmacologic attempt as the primary next strategy.

Adding chlorothiazide is a clinically meaningful competitor for less urgent diuretic resistance; switching loop drugs is another recognizable error. Their inferiority here comes from the current respiratory deterioration and observed response, not rhetorical option wording.

This supports escalation to extracorporeal support; it does not establish that CVVHD is universally superior to every intermittent or hybrid modality. No other replacement modality is offered, so that broader ranking is not required for this single best answer.

The earlier improvement followed by new positive balance, failed diuresis and escalating respiratory support is coherent. Current findings are sufficient independently of the earlier answer. Prior feedback does not explicitly supply this treatment choice.

The severity also requires ongoing urgent respiratory assessment. The renal intervention should not be read as a substitute for airway/ventilatory care; omission of an airway option does not create a second correct option in this renal-support comparison.
suggestions: No required repair to the offered comparison. Keep the explanation focused on the indication for urgent fluid removal and avoid inferring a universal modality preference from this item.

item.title: CRRT anticoagulation after bleeding and circuit clotting
fairness: Regional citrate is the best offered strategy: the resident must weigh persistent hemorrhage risk against demonstrated failure of anticoagulant-free circuits, then choose circuit anticoagulation that limits systemic exposure.

The circuit and bleeding observations make both competing errors meaningful. Avoiding anticoagulation is tempting after hemorrhage but has already interrupted needed therapy; systemic heparin addresses clotting at the cost of greater systemic anticoagulant exposure.

The current circulation and metabolic findings support considering citrate; they do not guarantee that citrate accumulation cannot occur. The explanation appropriately retains metabolic monitoring rather than declaring the strategy risk-free.

The options are parallel specific anticoagulation strategies. The word 'regional' requires relevant clinical understanding to distinguish it from systemic anticoagulation; it is not merely a uniquely cautious explanatory answer. Prior circuit failure is necessary treatment-response evidence, not a sufficient layperson cue to choose between the two remaining drugs.

The standalone record provides the named patient's age, sex, bleeding history, circuit course and current condition. It does not depend on either parked citrate comparison. This is a useful general-surgery ICU concept.
suggestions: No required repair. Keep the feedback's monitoring qualification and avoid broadening normal current lactate/bilirubin into an absolute safety rule.

item.title: Continuing a monitored interruption of CRRT

item.title: CRRT anticoagulation after bleeding and circuit clotting
fairness: Regional citrate is the best offered strategy: the resident must weigh persistent hemorrhage risk against demonstrated failure of anticoagulant-free circuits, then choose circuit anticoagulation that limits systemic exposure.

The circuit and bleeding observations make both competing errors meaningful. Avoiding anticoagulation is tempting after hemorrhage but has already interrupted needed therapy; systemic heparin addresses clotting at the cost of greater systemic anticoagulant exposure.

The current circulation and metabolic findings support considering citrate; they do not guarantee that citrate accumulation cannot occur. The explanation appropriately retains metabolic monitoring rather than declaring the strategy risk-free.

The options are parallel specific anticoagulation strategies. The word 'regional' requires relevant clinical understanding to distinguish it from systemic anticoagulation; it is not merely a uniquely cautious explanatory answer. Prior circuit failure is necessary treatment-response evidence, not a sufficient layperson cue to choose between the two remaining drugs.

The standalone record provides the named patient's age, sex, bleeding history, circuit course and current condition. It does not depend on either parked citrate comparison. This is a useful general-surgery ICU concept.
suggestions: No required repair. Keep the feedback's monitoring qualification and avoid broadening normal current lactate/bilirubin into an absolute safety rule.

item.title: Choose a valid fluid-response assessment
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 11 new executable nodes were reviewed using candidate presentations, updates, exhibits, tasks, option labels and explanations, including preceding visible explanations. No rewritten, kept-unchanged or retired executable records were present. The one unkeyed individualized-pressure-target hold and eight remaining research gaps were noted but not scored. Review-only keys and author self-assessments were not evidence of quality.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial and clinical-plausibility review, with no network or independent current-guideline verification. PASS does not establish source validity or clinical approval; every draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified exam-frequency claims.

Passive leg raising with direct stroke-volume measurement is the best offered assessment. The resident must reject the apparently actionable pulse-pressure variation because of acquisition conditions, then choose a measurement strategy compatible with those conditions. The respiratory diameter surrogate is a credible neighboring error but less dependable here.

The options have parallel verbs and comparable specificity. Neither the diagnosis label atrial fibrillation nor the displayed 22% supplies the answer without knowing the measurement assumptions. Repetition of variation does not uniquely identify the key.

The complete task, named 56-year-old patient and short complaint are present. The finite presentation repeats the same clinical context. This first node requires no preceding answer. The consultation wording is understandable as review of ICU care rather than a new clinic treatment encounter.
suggestions: Retain both the rhythm and spontaneous-effort observations; do not remove necessary acquisition information in an attempt to make the item harder.

If acquisition detail is expanded, ensure the direct flow measurement is reliable despite beat-to-beat variability; do not imply that any isolated stroke-volume reading is sufficient in atrial fibrillation.

Across the five cases, optional presentation polish is to state explicitly that the named patient remains in the ICU and that the clinic consultation reviews the record. Preserve age, sex and short visit reason. Runtime wait displays and randomization were not demonstrated by this text-only review.

item.title: Separate fluid responsiveness from fluid tolerance
fairness: Increasing norepinephrine is the best offered next adjustment: marked hypotension persists despite substantial measured output, while the respiratory course deteriorated after fluid. The reversible stroke-volume rise is a genuine competing reason to consider fluid, so the learner must distinguish responsiveness from whether pursuing it is beneficial.

A positive passive-leg-raise response does not compel a bolus. Conversely, B-lines alone would not prove fluid-induced hydrostatic edema; the recommendation is supported by the combined oxygen trajectory, examination, flow and pressure findings. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming a proved edema mechanism.
Dobutamine is less compelling with vigorous contraction and substantial output. It is the weaker distractor, but the fluid-versus-pressor decision remains a consequential, credible comparison.

The preceding explanation teaches how to assess responsiveness, not whether this patient should receive fluid. The new respiratory and flow findings change the decision. The current update supplies norepinephrine use, and the current exhibit and shared presentation are sufficient without remembering the prior answer.
The task names the relevant decision dimensions without supplying their interpretation. Option labels are short and parallel; no nonmedical wording shortcut was identified.
suggestions: Retain the positive reversible flow response and post-fluid respiratory deterioration together; their tension is the useful learning objective.

Keep the conclusion patient-specific. Do not generalize this example into a rule that B-lines always prohibit fluid or that positive fluid responsiveness always requires fluid. Exact clinical ranking remains for clinician sign-off.

item.title: Treat low flow despite restored arterial pressure
fairness: Dobutamine is the best offered adjustment. The learner must recognize that an acceptable arterial pressure has not restored perfusion, then select flow support in the presence of low cardiac index and newly weak contraction rather than simply escalating pressure or giving more fluid.

The current perfusion findings, cardiac index, echocardiographic change and absent preload response provide a coherent basis for ranking the options. The explanation appropriately says dobutamine is a supported option and calls for reassessment; it does not claim that all alternative inotropic strategies are prohibited.

The prior explanation supplies some scaffolding by distinguishing inadequate pressure from substantial output and by discussing absent fluid response. It does not state the present dobutamine answer. The new low-output phenotype reverses the earlier treatment rationale, so the sequence still requires application rather than literal recall of prior feedback.

All current pressures, drugs, perfusion findings and flow observations are present in this node. It can be answered with the shared presentation without remembering previous numbers. 'Later' makes the new cardiac findings temporally possible rather than contradicting the earlier vigorous contraction.
No label-length, wording-overlap or convergence shortcut was identified. The correct choice requires knowing what the observations mean and what the drugs do.
suggestions: Preserve the contrast between restored pressure and deteriorating perfusion, with measured low flow and a technically adequate preload assessment.

Repair the preceding node's ambiguous antimicrobial-course wording without adding a statement there that directly teaches when to choose dobutamine. Recheck this full sequence after any preceding-feedback revision.

item.title: Integrate persistent lactate elevation with improving perfusion
fairness: Maintaining the current MAP target is the best offered order. The learner must reconcile a still-elevated but falling lactate with improving bedside perfusion, then decide whether a further pressure or fluid intervention is justified.

The negative preload response weakens reflex volume loading; the improving examination and adequate current pressure weaken reflex target escalation. The explanation correctly leaves reassessment necessary rather than declaring the residual lactate harmless or proving a nonhypoperfusion cause.

The repeated 65 mm Hg value is necessary to compare maintaining versus changing the existing goal. It is not an unfair numeric match by itself: the main competing choice explicitly changes that goal, and the record must be interpreted to choose between them. The numerical labels do not create a convergent answer pattern.

The first node is self-contained with named age/sex, a short visit reason, a complete task and a coherent record. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered alternative was identified. This does not establish 65 mm Hg as the universal goal for all patients.
suggestions: Optional wording polish: replace 'on an unchanged norepinephrine target of 65 mm Hg' with a statement that the MAP goal is 65 mm Hg during norepinephrine treatment; the target is pressure, not drug dose.
Keep the falling trend and the actual bedside observations. Do not replace them with an authored conclusion that perfusion has normalized or teach that lactate can be disregarded.

item.title: Persistent low pressure with substantial flow during norepinephrine escalation
fairness: Adding vasopressin is the single defensible best offered adjustment. The near-unchanged stroke volumes during passive leg raising do not support another preload-directed bolus, and current cardiac output of 7.6 L/min does not support choosing dobutamine for a demonstrated low-flow problem. Persistent low pressure despite increasing norepinephrine favors additional vasopressor support among these choices.

Two consequential steps remain: integrate pressure, output and reversible preload response to identify the dominant treatment problem, then choose the matching escalation. The observations are not replaced with a diagnosis label. Changing the flow or preload-response pattern would change the ranking.

No unique wording match, length outlier, convergence pattern, rhetorical absolute or pre-answer teaching sentence identifies the key. The three choices are concrete resuscitation adjustments. Mentioning increasing norepinephrine is legitimate decision information; it does not itself eliminate the fluid and inotrope competitors without clinical knowledge.

The isolated task is complete with the shared presentation, update and exhibit. Source control progressing from under way to complete is coherent, and antibiotic treatment clearly continues. The earlier route explanation supplies neither this key nor its pressure-versus-flow reasoning. Earlier unchanged preload response makes the fluid distractor less tempting in sequence, but the fresh measured output and pressure course still support a distinct decision.

For sequence review only, the preserved following inotrope node explicitly introduces later deterioration, new low cardiac index and diffuse weak contraction after pressure is maintained. This is a coherent changed state, not a contradiction of the current output. The current Explanation does not name the next keyed treatment. No new verdict is assigned to that preserved node.

The concept is high-yield surgical critical-care physiology and vasoactive management. Moderate is a qualitative prediction, not a measured result; this is not a hard question for a resident who can interpret the supplied hemodynamics.

No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The unspecified norepinephrine dose does not create a competing correct answer within this option set; this review does not establish a universal dose threshold or rule for choosing vasopressin over further norepinephrine titration. Offline editorial PASS is not source verification or clinical approval; retain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: Preserve the measured flow, reversible response and support trajectory together. Do not replace them with an authored vasodilatory-shock conclusion or add an unsupported dose cutoff.
Retain the explicit later-state transition before the preserved inotrope question. Keep any expanded feedback from naming its next answer.

item.title: Choose a valid fluid-response assessment
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 11 new executable nodes were reviewed using candidate presentations, updates, exhibits, tasks, option labels and explanations, including preceding visible explanations. No rewritten, kept-unchanged or retired executable records were present. The one unkeyed individualized-pressure-target hold and eight remaining research gaps were noted but not scored. Review-only keys and author self-assessments were not evidence of quality.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial and clinical-plausibility review, with no network or independent current-guideline verification. PASS does not establish source validity or clinical approval; every draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified exam-frequency claims.

Passive leg raising with direct stroke-volume measurement is the best offered assessment. The resident must reject the apparently actionable pulse-pressure variation because of acquisition conditions, then choose a measurement strategy compatible with those conditions. The respiratory diameter surrogate is a credible neighboring error but less dependable here.

The options have parallel verbs and comparable specificity. Neither the diagnosis label atrial fibrillation nor the displayed 22% supplies the answer without knowing the measurement assumptions. Repetition of variation does not uniquely identify the key.

The complete task, named 56-year-old patient and short complaint are present. The finite presentation repeats the same clinical context. This first node requires no preceding answer. The consultation wording is understandable as review of ICU care rather than a new clinic treatment encounter.
suggestions: Retain both the rhythm and spontaneous-effort observations; do not remove necessary acquisition information in an attempt to make the item harder.

If acquisition detail is expanded, ensure the direct flow measurement is reliable despite beat-to-beat variability; do not imply that any isolated stroke-volume reading is sufficient in atrial fibrillation.

Across the five cases, optional presentation polish is to state explicitly that the named patient remains in the ICU and that the clinic consultation reviews the record. Preserve age, sex and short visit reason. Runtime wait displays and randomization were not demonstrated by this text-only review.

item.title: Separate fluid responsiveness from fluid tolerance
fairness: Increasing norepinephrine is the best offered next adjustment: marked hypotension persists despite substantial measured output, while the respiratory course deteriorated after fluid. The reversible stroke-volume rise is a genuine competing reason to consider fluid, so the learner must distinguish responsiveness from whether pursuing it is beneficial.

A positive passive-leg-raise response does not compel a bolus. Conversely, B-lines alone would not prove fluid-induced hydrostatic edema; the recommendation is supported by the combined oxygen trajectory, examination, flow and pressure findings. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming a proved edema mechanism.
Dobutamine is less compelling with vigorous contraction and substantial output. It is the weaker distractor, but the fluid-versus-pressor decision remains a consequential, credible comparison.

The preceding explanation teaches how to assess responsiveness, not whether this patient should receive fluid. The new respiratory and flow findings change the decision. The current update supplies norepinephrine use, and the current exhibit and shared presentation are sufficient without remembering the prior answer.
The task names the relevant decision dimensions without supplying their interpretation. Option labels are short and parallel; no nonmedical wording shortcut was identified.
suggestions: Retain the positive reversible flow response and post-fluid respiratory deterioration together; their tension is the useful learning objective.

Keep the conclusion patient-specific. Do not generalize this example into a rule that B-lines always prohibit fluid or that positive fluid responsiveness always requires fluid. Exact clinical ranking remains for clinician sign-off.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends the clinic after appendectomy and separate removal of two small nodules seen during the operation. The complete appendix specimen has a clear base margin and low-grade mucinous lining without infiltrative glands. The pelvic nodule contains fibrous tissue without mucinous epithelium. decisionNodes.stem: Which management pathway should be recommended for {patientName} after review of the separately labelled surgical specimens?

answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for follow-up without resection
answerChoices.rationale: Margin-negative noninfiltrative disease confined to an intact appendix could support this pathway. The separate diaphragmatic nodule contains mucinous epithelium, so the appendix margin and negative pelvic nodule cannot establish confinement.

answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for right hemicolectomy and nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The whole appendix does not show destructive glandular invasion requiring the localized adenocarcinoma nodal pathway. The demonstrated tumor is in a separate surface deposit; a regional colectomy does not by itself address that distribution.

answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for cytoreduction and intraperitoneal therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Low-grade mucinous epithelium in the separately labelled diaphragmatic nodule demonstrates cellular disease outside the appendix. This requires experienced-center assessment for cytoreduction with or without intraperitoneal treatment. Histology, extent and operative feasibility determine the final plan; the biopsy does not guarantee eligibility.

decisionNodes.explanation: The specimens represent different sites. A negative pelvic nodule and a clear appendiceal margin do not negate low-grade mucinous epithelium in the diaphragmatic nodule. That finding changes the disease field beyond the appendix. Experienced-center assessment for cytoreduction and possible intraperitoneal therapy is appropriate; this is not a promise of HIPEC or evidence that every deposit has been sampled. item.title: Site-specific pathology and mucinous peritoneal disease
fairness: The diaphragmatic nodule contains mucinous epithelium at a separate peritoneal site. The negative pelvic nodule and clear appendiceal margin do not invalidate that positive specimen. This interpretation changes the relevant disease field and supports specialist assessment for cytoreduction and intraperitoneal therapy.

The key is an assessment pathway, not an assertion that immediate cytoreduction or HIPEC is mandatory despite no bulky residual disease. The explanation preserves that important distinction. Follow-up may ultimately be selected by the specialist team, but it should not be predetermined from the negative pelvic specimen and postoperative imaging.

The two steps are resolving the site-specific sampling evidence, then selecting peritoneal-disease assessment rather than regional colectomy or a preselected observation pathway. Appendiceal mucinous peritoneal spread is a standard board-relevant concept even though the clinical condition is uncommon.

All three options share 'Multidisciplinary review for' and name a concrete subsequent pathway. No uniquely cautious generic key, meaningful length outlier, absolute wording or nonmedical convergence shortcut was identified. The mucin and epithelial descriptions require medical interpretation rather than directly repeating an answer label.
The case is standalone and includes the operative specimens, complete primary review and postoperative staging. No earlier explanation is needed to establish the separate diaphragmatic finding.
suggestions: Retain 'assessment' rather than guaranteed treatment in the explanation. Preserve the separate specimen labels; combining them into a global negative or positive summary would remove the interpretation being tested.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Dedicated liver MRI obtained after the staging CT resolves both previously indeterminate lesions. Each has uniform low T1 and high T2 signal, a smooth thin wall, and no mural nodule or enhancement on the acquired precontrast and postcontrast series. The remainder of liver MRI and chest, abdominal and pelvic staging shows no additional lesions. The whole appendix specimen contains a 2.6-cm well-differentiated grade-1 neuroendocrine tumor with a clear base margin; the mesoappendix was removed. {patientName} has recovered and remains fit for surgery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s appendiceal tumor after these acquired staging results?

answerChoices.label: Finish resection with appendectomy and follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The liver findings have benign cyst morphology, but the completely measured primary is larger than the guideline boundary for appendix-only treatment. A clear base does not address regional nodal risk.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with right hemicolectomy and regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The acquired MRI observations characterize the represented liver lesions as simple cysts rather than leaving them indeterminate for staging. In this fit patient, the whole-specimen tumor size supports regional resection despite a clear appendectomy margin.

answerChoices.label: Obtain liver core biopsy before further resection
answerChoices.rationale: These are resolved fluid-signal, nonenhancing lesions without internal solid tissue on adequate MRI, not persistent indeterminate targets. Biopsy would add an unsupported staging step. This conclusion comes from morphology, not a negative receptor scan.

A smaller favorable tumor or unresolved liver staging would change this decision.

item.title: Appendiceal NET resection after characterization of liver lesions

cues.why: Minor preinterpretation: 'resolves' announces that the prior uncertainty has been settled before the learner reads the morphology. It does not reveal whether the lesions are benign or metastatic and does not independently select the key, so this is an optional tightening rather than a blocking cue.

fairness: The MRI observations support simple cysts rather than a liver-biopsy requirement. The complete specimen then supplies a 2.6-cm well-differentiated NET, a clear base and a fit patient without demonstrated metastatic disease. Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes is the best offered plan under the usual size-based surgical teaching; no confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in this supplied scenario.

There are two consequential decisions: update the indeterminate CT findings using the acquired MRI morphology, then apply regional-resection reasoning despite favorable grade and a clear local margin. Incorrectly treating the lesions as unresolved changes the immediate action to biopsy; incorrectly equating a clear margin with adequate nodal treatment changes the action to follow-up.

The known neuroendocrine diagnosis is legitimate for a staging-and-management question. There is no need to hide it. The numerical tumor size is actual case data, not an invented probability or cutoff introduced by this review.

This is a standalone revision. Its presentation and update carry both the initial CT concern and the later MRI/pathology findings, with no dependence on the parked receptor-staging question. No preceding explanation supplies the MRI interpretation.
Appendiceal NET operative management is high yield. The liver imaging adds a meaningful staging issue rather than an unrelated second objective.
suggestions: For cleaner interpretation, replace 'resolves both previously indeterminate lesions' with a neutral statement that the MRI evaluates those same two lesions, followed by the current observations.
Remove 'directly sourced' from learner-facing feedback. Explain the clinical principle there and keep provenance language in the evidence records.

item.title: High-grade hepatic injury with stable physiology

cues.why: Nonblocking weakness: 'empiric' uniquely signals a less targeted intervention and may make this distractor easier to reject. It also identifies the actual proposed intervention in a record with no arterial target; it does not by itself distinguish observation from laparotomy. Do not count it as a source of difficulty.

fairness: Monitored nonoperative hepatic care is the best offered plan. The resident must weigh a substantial anatomic grade against serial stability and a nonperitoneal examination, then decide whether there is an indication for arterial intervention. Grade-driven surgery and unnecessary embolization are recognizable errors. This sits at the easier end of moderate, not hard; its value is the high-yield grade-versus-physiology decision.

'No arterial extravasation' and 'no blood/vasopressor requirement; hemoglobin unchanged' are essential management data. The observation choice is concrete in this historical hospital context, and 'empiric embolization' specifies a competing action rather than another umbrella nonoperative plan. No equally good alternative is apparent among these choices.

Maya's clinic attendance does not imply outpatient management of the recorded grade IV injury. The 42-year-old woman's presentation, exhibit and task are sufficient as the first node. The explanation appropriately limits its claim to grade not requiring laparotomy by itself; it does not claim that grade is irrelevant to monitoring or rescue planning. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The initial record does not reveal the later bleeding event. Its explanation mentions absence of a vascular focus but does not name the subsequent complication or its procedure. This creates some legitimate conceptual scaffolding without answering the next preserved node.
suggestions: Retain a monitored hospital plan and avoid converting this into outpatient observation merely because the patient now attends clinic.
If revising distractors later, reassess whether 'empiric' is needed to state the real competing plan; do not replace it with a vague angiography label that creates a new management ambiguity.

item.title: Delayed arterial bleeding into the biliary tract
fairness: Selective hepatic angiography and embolization is the best offered procedure. Papillary blood and a sac communicating with a hepatic arterial branch establish the bleeding pathway; maintained unsupported circulation then favors targeted endovascular control. ERCP is a plausible wrong-target response to a biliary presentation, while laparotomy treats bleeding with a more invasive route than this physiology requires. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

'Communicates with a hepatic arterial branch' is clinically necessary evidence. 'Hepatic' also appears in the operative alternative, so an organ-word match does not uniquely select the key. Understanding why a biliary stent does not control the described arterial source requires medical knowledge. Options are procedure labels of comparable scope without rationale-bearing qualifiers or rhetorical absolutes.

This is a high-yield complication and a moderate two-step task: localize the bleeding mechanism from the endoscopic/imaging relationship, then select its control method using the physiology. A familiar reader may recognize hemobilia quickly, but must still distinguish arterial control from treating the biliary lumen.

'During admission' clearly places the update within the historical hospitalization. The current update plus CT independently supplies the prior hepatic injury, present bleeding, arterial lesion and current physiology; the original injury grade and an earlier correct answer are not needed. The transition from initial observation is coherent. Earlier feedback does not prescribe embolization or give away this complication.
suggestions: Keep the papillary observation, arterial communication and current unsupported circulation visible when this later node is displayed independently.
Keep hemobilia/pseudoaneurysm diagnostic labels in post-answer teaching rather than adding them to the presentation or exhibit.

item.title: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage after arterial control
fairness: Preperitoneal pelvic packing is the best supplied rescue procedure. First interpret persistent shock after mechanical stabilization and completed arterial treatment as compatible with remaining venous/bony bleeding; then target the pelvic compartment rather than automatically repeat arterial treatment or explore the peritoneal cavity. This is a high-yield moderate sequence decision, not a claim that packing must always precede angiography.

The record supplies 'Selective pelvic arterial runs show no further extravasation' and 'no intraperitoneal injury' with ongoing instability. These findings weaken the competing routes, but interpreting a completion angiogram and distinguishing retroperitoneal from intraperitoneal control still requires clinical knowledge. Packing is not merely the sole untried choice: intraperitoneal exploration is also untried. No convincing nonmedical novelty, wording-match or length cue identifies the key.

A negative completion angiogram does not prove all arterial bleeding impossible. The explanation appropriately says residual bleeding 'can come from venous or bony sources.' Repeat embolization would be more competitive with a new arterial target or evidence the initial treatment was incomplete; neither is supplied. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the precise rescue sequence remains subject to clinician review rather than offline protocol verification.

Dylan's historical record contains the prior CT, stabilization, embolization and current condition in one exhibit, so the first node stands alone. The clinic frame does not ask the clinic to perform packing or establish a new capability requirement.
suggestions: Preserve the completed arterial treatment, continuing mechanical stabilization and exclusion of a competing intraperitoneal source.
Retain the conditional explanation; do not turn a negative completion angiogram into proof of a uniquely venous source or export this rescue order as a universal pelvic-trauma algorithm.

item.title: Recurrent arterial pelvic bleeding after packing
fairness: Pelvic angiography with embolization is the best offered procedure. The expanding pool connected to an arterial branch supplies a current target despite earlier benefit from packing. The resident must identify the changed bleeding component and change treatment rather than repeat the previously effective intervention. This supports a moderate two-step, high-yield judgment.

'Packing remains positioned' does not prove packing has controlled every source and does not prohibit repeat packing in other circumstances. The important discriminator is the new arterial-connected expanding pool. 'No new intraperitoneal abnormality' is a necessary compartment distinction, not a teaching statement. The key and packing alternative both name the pelvis; there is no unique plain-language location match or explanatory distractor that solves the item without medical interpretation.

The support trajectory is less detailed than in the splenic node, but 'BP remains 112/66 mmHg during support' describes maintained circulation rather than an isolated improved pressure, and CT has already localized the target. The key remains preferable among the supplied procedures. Do not infer a universal blood-pressure threshold or that needing transfusion is equivalent to being unsupported and stable. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The current update explicitly supplies prior packing, initial response, recurrent bleeding, ongoing support and new CT. It is answerable without remembering the earlier angiogram or selecting packing correctly. The later focal finding changes the correct action; prior feedback about possible venous/bony bleeding does not disclose this new arterial result. Historical 'now' remains clear under the clinic frame.
suggestions: If the wording is expanded in a future authorized revision, describe whether support needs are stable or escalating rather than adding an invented numeric eligibility cutoff.
Keep both the interval response to packing and the new vascular finding; neither an isolated pressure nor the fact of prior packing should become the whole decision rule.

item.title: Initial observation of a contained calyceal urine leak
fairness: Monitored nonoperative renal care is the best offered initial plan. The resident must interpret preserved perfusion and downstream urinary opacification alongside a calyceal leak, then distinguish this record from a disrupted outflow pathway or a complicated leak needing intervention. Automatic stenting of every extravasation and operative repair of a stable collecting-system injury are plausible overtreatment errors. This is a moderate, high-yield two-step task.

The raw finding 'Delayed images opacify the pelvis and ureter through to the bladder' preserves the need to interpret continuity. It does not say that the patient qualifies for observation. 'Without fever or an enlarging collection' supplies complication information needed to rank stenting. The alternatives have comparable procedural/care scope; no obvious phrase match, absolute, convergence or unusually qualified key solves the question without medical knowledge.

The explanation is acceptable for this initial decision, but absent fever and collection growth are not an exhaustive definition of every symptomatic leak. Neither the stem nor explanation should be generalized to worsening pain, ileus, obstruction or other evolving complications. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the stated initial management ranking.

The preceding revised renal explanation says what the complete CT protocol evaluates, including urinary continuity; it does not state the management of a calyceal leak. That is limited scaffolding, not the answer. The current update provides the completed study, urinary continuity, absence of arterial bleeding and stable course, so the preserved node stands alone and coherently follows initial imaging. Iris's age/sex and historical admission remain supplied by the clinic presentation.
suggestions: Preserve the initial-decision wording and the distinction between a small uncomplicated leak and an evolving symptomatic collection.
When teaching after the answer, avoid implying that fever and enlargement are the only reasons urinary extravasation might need intervention.

item.title: Procedure for distal pancreatic main-duct transection
fairness: Distal pancreatectomy is the preferred standard answer for the adult distal duct-disrupting injury described at laparotomy. The learner must integrate transection location and main-duct division, then select definitive surgery in a patient whose physiology permits it. Perfused distal tissue makes preservation/reconstruction tempting but does not restore duct continuity. The comparison with drainage and reconstruction makes this moderate rather than a mere anatomy-label question; duct status and location are high-yield trauma concepts.

'Left of superior mesenteric vessels' is necessary anatomical evidence rather than a literal match to 'Distal pancreatectomy.' 'Tissue toward the splenic hilum remains perfused' supports a real preservation temptation, and the normalizing physiology distinguishes definitive surgery from abbreviated care. There is no pre-answer instruction to preserve tissue, named diagnostic grade, absolute or length outlier selecting the key.

Pancreaticojejunostomy can be considered in selected circumstances; the best-answer ranking must not be taught as proof that reconstruction is impossible. No patient-specific feature here establishes such an exception to the standard distal resection approach. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the exact reconstructive comparison remains subject to clinician sign-off, not fresh source verification in this offline review.

The feedback explains duct disruption versus a duct-intact injury but does not address the closest preservation competitor. This limits teaching quality without making the question unanswerable. Miles's historical operative stage is explicit, and 'at this operation' prevents confusion with a clinic procedure. The node is standalone with the relevant anatomy and physiology supplied.
suggestions: Improve post-answer feedback by explaining why distal resection is preferred over pancreaticojejunostomy in the stated adult trauma setting, using verified claims and retaining selected reconstructive exceptions.
Do not invent an anatomic-length cutoff, contraindication or tissue-viability problem to dismiss reconstruction. Preserve the current duct, location and physiology findings.

item.title: Contained renal hematoma with a separate operative bleeding source

cues.phrase: Leave Gerota fascia and kidney undisturbed
cues.why: Nonblocking option-pattern risk: this is the sole 'Leave' choice against two 'Open Gerota fascia' choices. Its outlier status is visible without medical knowledge, but does not logically make it correct. The shared opening step represents two distinct renal interventions; adding a filler fourth option or obscuring the operative choices would not improve the item.

fairness: Leaving the renal compartment undisturbed is the best offered action. The resident must attribute the active bleeding to the identified mesenteric injury while interpreting a separately contained lateral hematoma, then resist opening that compartment merely because the patient is hypotensive. The unstable patient supplies a consequential competing consideration; this is a moderate two-step, high-yield blunt retroperitoneal-trauma decision.

'Stays the same size during exposure; no pulsation, free rupture or progressive expansion' is behavior that must be interpreted in the blunt lateral hematoma setting, not a statement that no renal intervention is indicated. The two opening options are distinct repair versus removal decisions, and the key is not the longest, most qualified or uniquely comprehensive option. The visible action outlier does not replace knowledge of the compartment rule and its exceptions.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation correctly limits the conclusion to a contained nonexpanding zone-II hematoma with a separate bleeding source. It should not be generalized to unexplained ongoing instability, a different mechanism, expanding or ruptured hematoma, or other retroperitoneal zones.

Noah's named age/sex presentation explicitly identifies historical laparotomy; the exhibit supplies the operation's indication, active source, current resuscitation and renal findings. 'During this exploration' remains a complete historical task. This standalone node requires no unseen earlier decision or eventual outcome, and the clinic reframing creates no contradiction.
suggestions: Retain the blunt mechanism, lateral location, observed hematoma behavior and identified separate bleeding source; these are the facts that prevent an unsafe blanket rule.
Do not manufacture option symmetry by adding an implausible fourth action. Recheck the leave/open pattern if a future clinically credible alternative is available.

item.title: Evolving symptoms after equivocal bowel-trauma CT
fairness: Repeat contrast-enhanced CT is the best of the offered plans: the resident must recognize a worsening trajectory after nonspecific initial findings, then distinguish the need for renewed investigation from either unchanged observation or immediate exploration.

The current update states the prior CT, elapsed interval, examination and hemodynamics. It stands alone and follows coherently from the preserved observation node. That earlier explanation recommends serial assessment but does not supply the repeat-CT answer.

The soft abdomen and absent involuntary guarding/rebound are necessary discrimination data, not gratuitous deletion of surgical danger signs. Increasing tenderness and tachycardia make unchanged serial examination a credible but less appropriate alternative.
No material wording, length, convergence, diagnostic-label or absolute-language shortcut identified. The prior CT is not a disposable foil: evolving findings give a reason to repeat it.

High-yield concept: recognition and reassessment of occult blunt bowel injury. The six-hour interval is case chronology, not a gameplay wait or a universal deadline. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Retain the trajectory and decision-critical examination findings. In clinician sign-off, confirm the intended boundary between repeat imaging and exploration without converting these fictional observations into numeric treatment thresholds.

item.title: Adequacy of bladder imaging after pelvic trauma
fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best offered study. The resident must infer that persistent gross hematuria with pelvic fracture needs bladder evaluation, then recognize that excreted contrast in an underfilled bladder does not supply an adequate cystogram.

The acquisition log establishes what was actually obtained; the item does not equate a missing exported image with a missing acquisition. Upper-tract opacification explains why simply extending an excretory CT pathway is the closest protocol error.
The catheter history makes routine retrograde urethrography a weaker initial answer without asserting that easy catheter passage or absent meatal blood absolutely excludes urethral injury.

'Bladder walls remain apposed' and 'bladder distension' are related, but interpreting their diagnostic significance requires protocol knowledge. No independent nonmedical wording shortcut strong enough to determine the answer was identified.

The node is self-contained. Its explanation teaches acquisition adequacy, not the following node's repair exception. This is a high-yield trauma-imaging distinction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Preserve the actual acquisition record and distinguish inadequate bladder evaluation from a negative result.
Do not expand the explanation into an absolute rule excluding urethral injury from the catheter observations.

item.title: Extraperitoneal bladder injury complicated by a bone fragment
fairness: Primary repair with urethral catheter drainage is the best offered plan. The resident must interpret the extraperitoneal leak distribution, then recognize that intraluminal bone makes the usual catheter-only approach inappropriate.

The urethral-catheter plan is a credible default for an uncomplicated extraperitoneal injury. Switching to suprapubic drainage does not remove the penetrating fragment, so it is a weaker but distinct management error.

The raw bony finding is decisive and must remain; it is not a diagnosis label or a wording match to the key. Options are parallel concrete bladder plans, with no uniquely long key, absolute-language cue or majority-component shortcut.

The update restates circulation, catheter function and current tests. It follows the preceding imaging question coherently and stands alone. Prior feedback about cystographic adequacy does not teach this treatment exception.

High-yield distinction: complicated versus uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder trauma. The stale 'intraperitoneal' identifier is not learner-visible evidence and was not used to infer the answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: In post-answer teaching, explicitly include management of the intraluminal bone fragment as part of repair so the explanation does not imply that closing around it is sufficient.
Preserve the extraperitoneal imaging findings and intact urethral drainage; do not turn the case into a simple intraperitoneal-rupture recall question.

item.title: Small jejunal defect with adjacent mesenteric devascularization
fairness: Resection with immediate anastomosis is the best offered plan. The small antimesenteric opening initially favors direct repair, but the torn mesentery and persistently nonviable-appearing adjacent bowel change the required extent of treatment.

The second consequential decision is reconstruction now versus staged discontinuity: perfused bowel beyond the injured segment, controlled bleeding, recovered physiology and lack of marked edema or diffuse soilage support immediate anastomosis.

The two resection choices prevent recognition of devascularization from completing the entire task. All options name the same jejunal site and are comparably specific; no material lexical, length, convergence or absolute-language shortcut identified.
The findings are deliberately decisive but clinically necessary. Do not misclassify all normal physiology as cueing when it distinguishes the deferred-reconstruction alternative.

This is a self-contained single-node case with a complete task. It tests high-yield small-bowel trauma decisions about viability and reconstruction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Retain the conflict between a small wall defect and a larger perfusion injury, as well as the separate reconstruction evidence.
Keep the fictional physiologic values as observations rather than presenting them as universal thresholds for anastomosis.

item.title: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage after arterial control
fairness: Preperitoneal pelvic packing is the best supplied rescue procedure. First interpret persistent shock after mechanical stabilization and completed arterial treatment as compatible with remaining venous/bony bleeding; then target the pelvic compartment rather than automatically repeat arterial treatment or explore the peritoneal cavity. This is a high-yield moderate sequence decision, not a claim that packing must always precede angiography.

The record supplies 'Selective pelvic arterial runs show no further extravasation' and 'no intraperitoneal injury' with ongoing instability. These findings weaken the competing routes, but interpreting a completion angiogram and distinguishing retroperitoneal from intraperitoneal control still requires clinical knowledge. Packing is not merely the sole untried choice: intraperitoneal exploration is also untried. No convincing nonmedical novelty, wording-match or length cue identifies the key.

A negative completion angiogram does not prove all arterial bleeding impossible. The explanation appropriately says residual bleeding 'can come from venous or bony sources.' Repeat embolization would be more competitive with a new arterial target or evidence the initial treatment was incomplete; neither is supplied. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the precise rescue sequence remains subject to clinician review rather than offline protocol verification.

Dylan's historical record contains the prior CT, stabilization, embolization and current condition in one exhibit, so the first node stands alone. The clinic frame does not ask the clinic to perform packing or establish a new capability requirement.
suggestions: Preserve the completed arterial treatment, continuing mechanical stabilization and exclusion of a competing intraperitoneal source.
Retain the conditional explanation; do not turn a negative completion angiogram into proof of a uniquely venous source or export this rescue order as a universal pelvic-trauma algorithm.

item.title: Recurrent arterial pelvic bleeding after packing
fairness: Pelvic angiography with embolization is the best offered procedure. The expanding pool connected to an arterial branch supplies a current target despite earlier benefit from packing. The resident must identify the changed bleeding component and change treatment rather than repeat the previously effective intervention. This supports a moderate two-step, high-yield judgment.

'Packing remains positioned' does not prove packing has controlled every source and does not prohibit repeat packing in other circumstances. The important discriminator is the new arterial-connected expanding pool. 'No new intraperitoneal abnormality' is a necessary compartment distinction, not a teaching statement. The key and packing alternative both name the pelvis; there is no unique plain-language location match or explanatory distractor that solves the item without medical interpretation.

The support trajectory is less detailed than in the splenic node, but 'BP remains 112/66 mmHg during support' describes maintained circulation rather than an isolated improved pressure, and CT has already localized the target. The key remains preferable among the supplied procedures. Do not infer a universal blood-pressure threshold or that needing transfusion is equivalent to being unsupported and stable. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The current update explicitly supplies prior packing, initial response, recurrent bleeding, ongoing support and new CT. It is answerable without remembering the earlier angiogram or selecting packing correctly. The later focal finding changes the correct action; prior feedback about possible venous/bony bleeding does not disclose this new arterial result. Historical 'now' remains clear under the clinic frame.
suggestions: If the wording is expanded in a future authorized revision, describe whether support needs are stable or escalating rather than adding an invented numeric eligibility cutoff.
Keep both the interval response to packing and the new vascular finding; neither an isolated pressure nor the fact of prior packing should become the whole decision rule.

item.title: Adequacy of bladder imaging after pelvic trauma
fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best offered study. The resident must infer that persistent gross hematuria with pelvic fracture needs bladder evaluation, then recognize that excreted contrast in an underfilled bladder does not supply an adequate cystogram.

The acquisition log establishes what was actually obtained; the item does not equate a missing exported image with a missing acquisition. Upper-tract opacification explains why simply extending an excretory CT pathway is the closest protocol error.
The catheter history makes routine retrograde urethrography a weaker initial answer without asserting that easy catheter passage or absent meatal blood absolutely excludes urethral injury.

'Bladder walls remain apposed' and 'bladder distension' are related, but interpreting their diagnostic significance requires protocol knowledge. No independent nonmedical wording shortcut strong enough to determine the answer was identified.

The node is self-contained. Its explanation teaches acquisition adequacy, not the following node's repair exception. This is a high-yield trauma-imaging distinction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Preserve the actual acquisition record and distinguish inadequate bladder evaluation from a negative result.
Do not expand the explanation into an absolute rule excluding urethral injury from the catheter observations.

items.value: Leaked contrast remains in tissue between the bladder and pubic symphysis and tracks beside the bladder. It does not outline bowel loops above the pelvis.

items.label: Inspection
items.value: A pointed fragment continuous with the fractured pubic bone projects through the anterior bladder wall into the lumen. The bladder neck and ureteral orifices are intact.

answerChoices.label: Primary bladder repair with urethral catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The distribution is extraperitoneal, but bone protruding through the bladder wall makes this more than an uncomplicated leak. Repair addresses the injury rather than relying on catheter drainage to heal around the persistent bony lesion.

answerChoices.label: Bladder drainage by urethral catheter with cystographic reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This is a supported pathway for an uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture. The projected bone fragment is the important exception; preserved catheter flow does not remove it.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a supported pathway for an uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture. The projected bone fragment is the important exception; preserved catheter flow does not remove it.

answerChoices.label: Bladder drainage by suprapubic catheter with cystographic reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Changing the drainage route does not address the bony lesion through the bladder wall. A suprapubic catheter can provide drainage in selected nonoperative injuries, but it is not a substitute for repair of this complexity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Changing the drainage route does not address the bony lesion through the bladder wall. A suprapubic catheter can provide drainage in selected nonoperative injuries, but it is not a substitute for repair of this complexity.

question.explanation: The distribution is extraperitoneal, but bone protruding through the bladder wall makes this more than an uncomplicated leak. Repair addresses the injury rather than relying on catheter drainage to heal around the persistent bony lesion.

concept.displayName: Complicated extraperitoneal bladder repair
concept.learningObjective: Choose repair rather than a routine catheter pathway for an extraperitoneal bladder injury with an intravesical bone fragment.

item.title: Extraperitoneal bladder injury complicated by a bone fragment
fairness: Primary repair with urethral catheter drainage is the best offered plan. The resident must interpret the extraperitoneal leak distribution, then recognize that intraluminal bone makes the usual catheter-only approach inappropriate.

The urethral-catheter plan is a credible default for an uncomplicated extraperitoneal injury. Switching to suprapubic drainage does not remove the penetrating fragment, so it is a weaker but distinct management error.

The raw bony finding is decisive and must remain; it is not a diagnosis label or a wording match to the key. Options are parallel concrete bladder plans, with no uniquely long key, absolute-language cue or majority-component shortcut.

The update restates circulation, catheter function and current tests. It follows the preceding imaging question coherently and stands alone. Prior feedback about cystographic adequacy does not teach this treatment exception.

High-yield distinction: complicated versus uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder trauma. The stale 'intraperitoneal' identifier is not learner-visible evidence and was not used to infer the answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: In post-answer teaching, explicitly include management of the intraluminal bone fragment as part of repair so the explanation does not imply that closing around it is sufficient.
Preserve the extraperitoneal imaging findings and intact urethral drainage; do not turn the case into a simple intraperitoneal-rupture recall question.

decisionNodes.stem: Which pancreatic procedure should be selected for {patientName} at this operation?

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Transection left of the mesenteric vessels involving the main duct is a distal duct-disrupting injury. Guidelines support distal resection rather than treating it as a duct-intact contusion.

answerChoices.label: External peripancreatic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Drainage can treat selected minor duct-intact injuries but leaves the disrupted distal duct source untreated in this complete transection.

answerChoices.label: Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Reconstructive preservation may be considered in selected proximal injuries; it is not the routine preferred approach for this distal complete transection.

item.title: Procedure for distal pancreatic main-duct transection
fairness: Distal pancreatectomy is the preferred standard answer for the adult distal duct-disrupting injury described at laparotomy. The learner must integrate transection location and main-duct division, then select definitive surgery in a patient whose physiology permits it. Perfused distal tissue makes preservation/reconstruction tempting but does not restore duct continuity. The comparison with drainage and reconstruction makes this moderate rather than a mere anatomy-label question; duct status and location are high-yield trauma concepts.

'Left of superior mesenteric vessels' is necessary anatomical evidence rather than a literal match to 'Distal pancreatectomy.' 'Tissue toward the splenic hilum remains perfused' supports a real preservation temptation, and the normalizing physiology distinguishes definitive surgery from abbreviated care. There is no pre-answer instruction to preserve tissue, named diagnostic grade, absolute or length outlier selecting the key.

Pancreaticojejunostomy can be considered in selected circumstances; the best-answer ranking must not be taught as proof that reconstruction is impossible. No patient-specific feature here establishes such an exception to the standard distal resection approach. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the exact reconstructive comparison remains subject to clinician sign-off, not fresh source verification in this offline review.

The feedback explains duct disruption versus a duct-intact injury but does not address the closest preservation competitor. This limits teaching quality without making the question unanswerable. Miles's historical operative stage is explicit, and 'at this operation' prevents confusion with a clinic procedure. The node is standalone with the relevant anatomy and physiology supplied.
suggestions: Improve post-answer feedback by explaining why distal resection is preferred over pancreaticojejunostomy in the stated adult trauma setting, using verified claims and retaining selected reconstructive exceptions.
Do not invent an anatomic-length cutoff, contraindication or tissue-viability problem to dismiss reconstruction. Preserve the current duct, location and physiology findings.

decisionNodes.stem: What renal surgical action should be taken for {patientName} during this exploration?

answerChoices.label: Leave Gerota fascia and kidney undisturbed
answerChoices.rationale: This renal hematoma remains contained and nonexpanding while a separate injury accounts for active bleeding. Instability alone does not require opening a stable zone-II hematoma.

answerChoices.label: Open Gerota fascia and repair the kidney
answerChoices.rationale: An unchanged contained hematoma with a separate active source does not establish a need for renal exploration. Expansion or demonstrable renal hemorrhage would change that assessment.

answerChoices.label: Open Gerota fascia and remove the kidney
answerChoices.rationale: Automatic nephrectomy is not supported by an unchanged hematoma with a separate active source; even required intervention may permit preservation.

item.title: Contained renal hematoma with a separate operative bleeding source

cues.phrase: Leave Gerota fascia and kidney undisturbed
cues.why: Nonblocking option-pattern risk: this is the sole 'Leave' choice against two 'Open Gerota fascia' choices. Its outlier status is visible without medical knowledge, but does not logically make it correct. The shared opening step represents two distinct renal interventions; adding a filler fourth option or obscuring the operative choices would not improve the item.

fairness: Leaving the renal compartment undisturbed is the best offered action. The resident must attribute the active bleeding to the identified mesenteric injury while interpreting a separately contained lateral hematoma, then resist opening that compartment merely because the patient is hypotensive. The unstable patient supplies a consequential competing consideration; this is a moderate two-step, high-yield blunt retroperitoneal-trauma decision.

'Stays the same size during exposure; no pulsation, free rupture or progressive expansion' is behavior that must be interpreted in the blunt lateral hematoma setting, not a statement that no renal intervention is indicated. The two opening options are distinct repair versus removal decisions, and the key is not the longest, most qualified or uniquely comprehensive option. The visible action outlier does not replace knowledge of the compartment rule and its exceptions.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation correctly limits the conclusion to a contained nonexpanding zone-II hematoma with a separate bleeding source. It should not be generalized to unexplained ongoing instability, a different mechanism, expanding or ruptured hematoma, or other retroperitoneal zones.

Noah's named age/sex presentation explicitly identifies historical laparotomy; the exhibit supplies the operation's indication, active source, current resuscitation and renal findings. 'During this exploration' remains a complete historical task. This standalone node requires no unseen earlier decision or eventual outcome, and the clinic reframing creates no contradiction.
suggestions: Retain the blunt mechanism, lateral location, observed hematoma behavior and identified separate bleeding source; these are the facts that prevent an unsafe blanket rule.
Do not manufacture option symmetry by adding an implausible fourth action. Recheck the leave/open pattern if a future clinically credible alternative is available.

decisionNodes.stem: At the documented laparotomy, which bowel plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s jejunal injury?

answerChoices.label: Jejunal resection with immediate anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: The small wall opening understates the injury: the separated mesentery and nonrecovering segment require resection. Healthy adjacent bowel and restored physiology support reconstruction rather than leaving a staged discontinuity in this record.

answerChoices.label: Jejunal repair with direct suture closure
answerChoices.rationale: Suture closure would address the visible opening but leave the segment whose perfusion has not recovered after mesenteric separation.

answerChoices.label: Jejunal resection with deferred reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Staged reconstruction can be appropriate when physiology, perfusion or ongoing control tasks remain unresolved. The current healthy margins and restored course support completing continuity rather than defaulting to discontinuity.

decisionNodes.explanation: The small wall opening understates the injury: the separated mesentery and nonrecovering segment require resection. Healthy adjacent bowel and restored physiology support reconstruction rather than leaving a staged discontinuity in this record.

items.label: Bowel examination
items.value: The antimesenteric opening involves about one fifth of the circumference. Across the adjacent segment, mesentery is torn away from the bowel. That segment remains grey and noncontractile after nearby bowel becomes pink with warming; its cut margins do not bleed. Bowel beyond both ends is pink with visible mesenteric pulsation.

items.label: Current physiology
items.value: Bleeding is controlled; BP 124/72 mmHg, temperature 36.8 C and pH 7.36. There is no further blood or vasopressor requirement, marked bowel edema or diffuse soilage.

fairness: Resection with immediate anastomosis is the best offered plan. The small antimesenteric opening initially favors direct repair, but the torn mesentery and persistently nonviable-appearing adjacent bowel change the required extent of treatment.

The second consequential decision is reconstruction now versus staged discontinuity: perfused bowel beyond the injured segment, controlled bleeding, recovered physiology and lack of marked edema or diffuse soilage support immediate anastomosis.

The two resection choices prevent recognition of devascularization from completing the entire task. All options name the same jejunal site and are comparably specific; no material lexical, length, convergence or absolute-language shortcut identified.
The findings are deliberately decisive but clinically necessary. Do not misclassify all normal physiology as cueing when it distinguishes the deferred-reconstruction alternative.

This is a self-contained single-node case with a complete task. It tests high-yield small-bowel trauma decisions about viability and reconstruction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; PASS is editorial only.
suggestions: Retain the conflict between a small wall defect and a larger perfusion injury, as well as the separate reconstruction evidence.
Keep the fictional physiologic values as observations rather than presenting them as universal thresholds for anastomosis.

fairness: The learner must recognize return to a compensated chronic baseline rather than demand normal PaCO2, then choose immediate post-extubation support for an older patient with chronic respiratory disease and hypercapnia during the trial. Both observations affect the plan.

Standard oxygen is a credible alternative because low-flow oxygen meets the recorded oxygenation need; preventive ventilatory support requires an additional risk-based inference. Continued intubation represents a recognizable error about chronic PaCO2 rather than an arbitrary absurd option.

Immediate bilevel support is a defensible best choice for this selected profile, and the explanation appropriately avoids ranking all possible HFNC/NIV combinations or extending prophylaxis to every extubation. item.title: Interpreting an SBT performed at higher oxygen concentration
fairness: The before/during table makes both support withdrawal and oxygen escalation visible. Calling the trial ?recorded as tolerated? is a report to evaluate, not proof that all extubation criteria were satisfied.

An unassisted trial is a valid method. Better saturation at higher FiO2 does not establish tolerance at the earlier concentration. Repeating at the earlier FiO2 is the best offered way to resolve that uncertainty; adding pressure support while retaining the higher FiO2 does not resolve it, and immediate extubation relies on an incompletely assessed oxygen condition.

The explanation correctly identifies its recommendation as conditional and very low certainty. Treat this as the best assessment among the offered plans, not proof of actual SBT failure, a universal extubation prohibition at FiO2 0.60, or a universal requirement for zero pressure support. This offline review cannot newly verify the exact recommendation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which respiratory-support plan best fits Elena Marsh’s recorded post-extubation deterioration?

answerChoices.label: Reintubate and resume invasive ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: The record now shows established worsening post-extubation respiratory failure in the population where rescue NIV may delay needed reintubation.

answerChoices.label: Begin rescue bilevel mask ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: Preventive NIV evidence does not justify delaying reintubation for established failure in this non-COPD medical record.

answerChoices.label: Escalate high-flow nasal oxygen
answerChoices.rationale: Further oxygen-focused support does not resolve the worsening ventilation and fatigue already present.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is rescue after deterioration, not prevention immediately after planned extubation. In general non-COPD medical patients with established post-extubation failure, ERS/ATS conditionally discourages NIV that may delay reintubation. The worsening ventilation and fatigue make continued oxygen escalation inadequate in this record. COPD and postoperative exceptions must not be erased.

claims.limitation: Distribution alone does not establish cause or bowel viability.
